722.title: Ashvaghosha himself
722.hook: a brahmin-born poet and monk, remembered also for the poem of Nanda
722.howItsDone: Ashvaghosha's poems are read today in Sanskrit classes and in translation by students of Buddhism and of Indian literature, and the story of Nanda is retold in Buddhist teaching about craving and letting go.

segments.voice: Yesterday: final nirvana, and the poem's ending kept in Tibetan and Chinese. Your line, the poem traveled. Today, the person who wrote it.

For weeks now, there's been a voice behind every scene. The king's fear in the palace. The worms in the plowed field. The gates swinging open without a sound. Mara's flowers. The long night under the tree. Someone chose every one of those pictures, and the words to hold them. His name is Ashvaghosha. And here's the honest part: we know very little about him. We have a short signature at the end of his poems, a handful of later stories, and the poems themselves.
screen: `A VOICE BEHIND EVERY SCENE.` → `HIS NAME: ASHVAGHOSHA.` → `WE KNOW VERY LITTLE.`

segments.voice: First, the signature. At the close of his other long poem, the author names himself: Ashvaghosha of Saketa, son of a woman named Suvarnakshi, a monk, a great poet and speaker. His town, his mother's name, and that he wore the robe. Not much more. Second, the brahmin. Later tradition says he was born a brahmin and trained in the old learning before he became a follower of the Buddha. His poems seem to agree. They are full of the old kings, sages and heroes of the Indian epics, used the way a well-read writer drops in names a learned audience will know. He doesn't throw that learning away. He puts it to work. Third, the poem of Nanda. His other surviving poem tells of Nanda, the Buddha's half-brother, newly married to a beautiful wife, Sundari, and deeply in love. The Buddha brings him into the order, and Nanda is miserable, thinking only of her. The poem follows him patiently, through longing, through a strange journey to see heavenly women, and on, step by step, until he lets go of craving altogether and finds peace. It's a poem about someone who did not want to be a monk, and how he got there anyway. Fourth, the monk who wrote. Put the pieces together and you get an unusual figure: a monk who lived by a discipline of simplicity, and who also wrote richly ornate verse. He didn't see those as opposites. A poet monk. Tomorrow, in his own words, why.

723.title: Why a poem
723.hook: teaching through beauty: he wrote so people would stay for the teaching
723.howItsDone: Buddhist communities also teach through story, verse and art: temple murals of the Buddha's life, chanted verses, and retellings of the birth stories, often alongside plain instruction in the teaching.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Ashvaghosha himself, a simple robe and rich verse, and your line, a poet monk. Today the poet tells us why he wrote.

A spoonful of honey, and under it, something bitter. It's an old trick with children: the medicine goes down because something sweet goes with it. A monk used the same picture to explain his writing. At the very end of the poem of Nanda, after all the longing, the journey and the letting go, Ashvaghosha steps out from behind the story and talks to the reader directly. He explains why a monk would write poetry at all.
screen: `HONEY OVER SOMETHING BITTER.` → `THE POET STEPS OUT.` → `WHY WRITE POETRY AT ALL?`

segments.voice: First, the purpose. He says the poem is about liberation, and that he wrote it not to give pleasure but to bring calm. The beauty was never the point. Second, the audience. He wrote in this ornate style, he says, to catch listeners whose minds are on other things. People who would never sit through a plain teaching might sit through a love affair, a king, a heavenly journey, and stay long enough to hear what it was really about. Third, the honey. Then the picture: just as bitter medicine is mixed with honey so it can be swallowed, he has mixed the teaching with poetry. Whatever in the poem is about liberation is the medicine. The rest, the descriptions, the music of the verse, is there to help it go down. Fourth, the gold. He asks readers to take what leads to peace and leave the rest, the way someone panning for gold keeps the gold and lets the dust wash away. So the honey is honest about being honey. He isn't hiding the teaching. He's telling you exactly where it is. He said this about the poem of Nanda, but hold the same idea up to the life we've heard these weeks. The empty saddle, the birds in one tree for a night, the dog with a dry bone, the torch of straw. Each one is honey around something hard: parting, grief, craving, and the way out. The poet hoped his listeners would stay for the beauty, and then keep the gold.

724.title: The poem, closed
724.hook: the life once more, now in verse
724.howItsDone: The Buddha's life is retold again and again in Buddhist cultures: in temple murals and carvings, in festival plays and chanting, and in children's books, each telling choosing its own scenes and its own light.

segments.voice: Yesterday: honey, medicine mixed with verse so it goes down, and your line, beauty carries it. Today we close the book on the poem.

Back in year one, the Buddha's life came to us in plain pieces: a birth, the sights on the road, a night ride, a tree, a first teaching, a last journey. This block told the same life again, slowly, through one poet's eyes. Same story, different light. It's like walking a road you know by heart, but at dawn, with someone who stops to point at things you'd walked past. Today, one last walk down the whole road, and a look at what the verse added.
screen: `THE SAME LIFE, TOLD TWICE.` → `A KNOWN ROAD, AT DAWN.` → `ONE LAST WALK.`

segments.voice: First, the palace. A queen's dream, a birth in a grove, an old sage weeping because he won't live to hear the boy teach. A father who fills the palace with music because he is afraid. In the poem, the walls are made of love, and that's what makes them hard to leave. Second, the road out. The sights the king tried to hide. The worms in the plowed furrow, grieved for like family. A refused request, a sleeping palace, gates that open on their own, a horse and a faithful attendant sent home. The poem lets every goodbye hurt. Third, the search and the night. Arguments from ministers, half a kingdom offered by a king, teachers who are good but not final, a bowl of milk-rice after the fasting. Then Mara with his flowered bow and his army, scattered, and a night of knowing, watch by watch, until dawn. Fourth, the turning and the end. Five old companions who rise despite themselves. Friends, fire-keepers, kings, a great ascetic arriving late. And in the Tibetan and Chinese, the rest: the last journey, the sala trees, the relics shared. That's the life, retold. What did the verse add? Not new facts, mostly. It added time to feel things. A father's fear. A wife's question. A prince's grief over worms. In the poem of Nanda, the poet said he wrote so people would stay for the teaching. All these days on one poem is a long stay. Next, the path turns from the teacher to the people who followed him, beginning with two friends at a festival.

725.title: Two friends at the festival
725.hook: Upatissa and Kolita watch a festival and suddenly find it empty
725.howItsDone: Sariputta and Moggallana are honored as the Buddha's two chief disciples; in some Theravada temples images of the two stand on either side of the Buddha, and their story is told in sermons and at festivals.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the poem, closed, the whole life told once more, and your line, the life, retold. Today a new block begins: the great disciples, the people who followed him.

Same seats as last year. Same hill above the city. Same crowd, same plays, same music, same jokes landing in the same places. Two young men from good families sit side by side in the best seats, as they always do at this festival. Other years, they laughed at the funny parts, cried at the sad ones and threw gifts to the performers. This year, the jokes land, and neither of them laughs. The sad scene plays, and neither of them cries. Each glances over and sees the other has gone quiet too.
screen: `SAME SEATS, SAME HILL.` → `THE JOKES LAND, NOBODY LAUGHS.` → `BOTH OF THEM, QUIET.`

segments.voice: First, the two friends. Their names are Upatissa and Kolita. The commentaries say they were sons of brahmin families from villages near Rajagaha, close friends since childhood, each with a circle of young companions around him. Later they'll be known by other names, Sariputta and Moggallana. But not yet. Right now they're two well-off young men at a festival. Second, the silence. The commentary tells it simply. Kolita turns to his friend: you don't seem to be enjoying yourself today. What's wrong? And Upatissa answers with a question of his own: what is there to look at here? Before long, all these people, the actors, the crowd, the two of them, will be gone. And here we sit, laughing. Third, the turn. Kolita has been thinking the same thing. Neither talked the other into it. They arrived at the same emptiness, in the same seats, on the same afternoon. Nothing about the festival was worse. What had changed was them. Fourth, the question that's left. They don't stay sad, and they don't go home and pretend. They decide, together, to look for a way out of birth and death, a release the festival can't give. Notice how close this sits to the prince's own story. He saw an old man, a sick man, a dead man, and the palace music went flat. These two never leave their seats. The emptiness finds them in the middle of the fun.

726.title: A pact
726.hook: whoever finds the deathless first will tell the other
726.howItsDone: Buddhist teaching gives great weight to good friendship; in the discourses the Buddha calls admirable friendship the whole of the holy life (SN 45.2), and in some communities monks and lay people practice in small groups who support each other.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Upatissa and Kolita, gone quiet at the festival, and your line, the show was empty. Today the two friends set out.

Two hikers reach a fork in a trail at dusk and agree to split up. Whoever finds the way down first comes back for the other. It's a simple deal, and it only works if both of them would really come back. Upatissa and Kolita make a deal like that, not about a trail, but about the deepest thing they can name. They've left the festival and their families' comforts to live as wanderers. And along the way they make each other a promise that will shape the rest of their lives.
screen: `A FORK IN THE TRAIL.` → `WHOEVER FINDS IT, COMES BACK.` → `THE TWO FRIENDS PROMISE.`

segments.voice: First, the teacher. In Rajagaha lives a wandering teacher named Sanjaya, with a large following of wanderers. The two friends go forth under him. The commentaries say they quickly learned everything he had to teach, and then asked: is there more? There wasn't. In another discourse, Sanjaya is remembered for answers that slip away when you reach for them: asked a hard question, he would say neither yes, nor no, nor neither. For these two, that was not a place to stop. Second, the word. What were they looking for? The Vinaya uses one word for it: the deathless. In Pali, amata. Not long life. Not a heaven that might end. The deathless names freedom from the whole round of birth and death, the thing the festival couldn't give. Third, the pact. As the Vinaya tells it, the two had given their word to each other: whoever reaches the deathless first will tell the other. No conditions. No race. No prize for winning. Just: if I get there, you'll hear of it. Fourth, why it matters. A seeker could easily turn inward and forget everyone else. These two built friendship into the search itself; each one's freedom was tied to the other's. And the pact assumes something: that one of them might get there without the other, and that whoever did would not be too proud, too busy or too far gone to come back. Tomorrow, one of them finds something.

727.title: The verse passed on
727.hook: Upatissa hears Assaji's verse, understands, and runs to tell Kolita (Vinaya, Mahavagga 1)
727.howItsDone: Assaji's verse is recited in Buddhist communities as a summary of the teaching, and the story of the two friends is told at temples and in Dhamma talks as the beginning of the Buddha's chief pair of disciples.

segments.voice: Yesterday: a pact. Whoever reaches the deathless first will tell the other, and your line, whoever finds it first. Today, one of them finds it.

Kolita sees his friend coming from a distance, and something has already changed. Not a word has been said. It's in Upatissa's face. The Vinaya, the monks' book of discipline, tells it simply: Kolita sees that his friend looks calm and clear, and asks him straight out whether he has found the deathless, the thing they both left home to look for. And Upatissa says yes. Earlier on this path we followed Upatissa behind a quiet monk named Assaji and heard the short verse Assaji gave him. Today is the other half of that morning: what Upatissa did with it.
screen: `A CHANGED FACE.` → `HAVE YOU FOUND IT?` → `YES, FRIEND.`

segments.voice: Start with where he went. Upatissa had just understood the thing he left home to look for. He could have stayed to question Assaji, or gone straight to find the Buddha. Instead he went to Kolita, because that was the pact. The verse was small enough to carry at a run. In paraphrase: of things that arise from a cause, the Buddha has told the cause, and also how they cease. Next, what he passed on. Not his own summary. Not a better version. He gave Kolita the same lines he'd heard, and the text says that on hearing them, Kolita understood too. Then they thought of someone else. Their old teacher, Sanjaya, still led a crowd of students, so the two went back and invited him to come with them. He refused, and offered instead to share the leadership of his group. They said no to that and left, and the Vinaya says many of his students went with them. Last, the arrival. The text says the Buddha saw the two friends coming from far off and told the monks, in paraphrase: these two will be my chief pair of disciples. Upatissa would be called Sariputta, and Kolita, Moggallana. Here's what the story keeps doing. Everyone in it who finds something good turns around and hands it on. Assaji to Upatissa. Upatissa to Kolita. Both of them to their old teacher. The verse travels because nobody sits on it.

728.title: The general of the dhamma
728.hook: Sariputta, foremost in wisdom, who could explain what the Buddha said briefly
728.howItsDone: In Theravada communities Sariputta is honored as the chief disciple in wisdom, and his discourses in the Pali texts are studied as models of how to explain the teaching step by step.

segments.voice: Yesterday: deathless, and Upatissa running to tell Kolita. Your line, he ran to tell him. Today, the friend who ran becomes the one who explains.

A brahmin named Sela has just met the Buddha, and he is won over. He is also a practical man. A teacher this great, he reasons, must have someone at his side who carries the work forward, the way a king has a general. So, in the Sutta Nipata, Sela asks it in verse: who is your general? Which disciple follows the teacher and keeps this going? It's a fair question about any movement. Somebody has to explain the thing when the founder isn't in the room. The Buddha answers with one name.
screen: `SELA IS WON OVER.` → `WHO IS YOUR GENERAL?` → `ONE NAME.`

segments.voice: First, the name: Sariputta. In paraphrase, the Buddha tells Sela: the wheel of the teaching that I set rolling, Sariputta keeps rolling, the one who comes after me. That's where the picture of a general comes from. Not a battle. A wheel that needs someone to keep it moving. Later tradition turned it into a title: the general of the dhamma. Second, what he was known for. In the Anguttara Nikaya's list of foremost disciples, the Buddha names Sariputta foremost in great wisdom. And in the discourses his wisdom has a recognizable shape: the Buddha says something short, and Sariputta opens it up so others can use it. Third, one scene of that. In the Samyutta Nikaya, a group of monks is about to leave for a far western country. The Buddha tells them: before you go, take leave of Sariputta. He's wise, and he helps his fellow monks. So they go to him, and he gets them ready. Out there, he says, wise people will question you. They'll ask what your teacher teaches. Answer simply: the removal of desire and lust. And if they ask, desire for what? Tell them: for the body, for feelings, for perceptions, for the rest of what we take ourselves to be. One plain line first, then the next step only if someone asks for it. That is the general at work: not commanding, but equipping. This week ran from Ashvaghosha himself, through honey, the poem closed, Upatissa, a pact and deathless, to today: the one who explains.
screen: `WHO KEEPS THE WHEEL ROLLING?` · `FOREMOST IN GREAT WISDOM.` · `GETTING TRAVELERS READY.` · `ONE PLAIN LINE FIRST.` · then, large: `WISDOM EXPLAINS.`

segments.voice: Pick something you understand well, how to make rice, what a word on this path means, and explain it silently the way Sariputta coached the travelers: one plain sentence, then stop. Imagine someone asking what you mean, give only the next sentence, and come back to the breath.
Sariputta. The disciple the Buddha named, when Sela asked who kept the wheel of the teaching rolling, foremost in wisdom, who readied others to explain it simply.
Your line: wisdom explains. One plain line first; the next only if someone asks. Day seven hundred twenty-eight, done.

He had been a soldier before, and he led the monks like troops.
He made the rules for the monks and punished anyone who broke them.
